This flexibility and ease of use position Router as a practical tool for developers seeking optimized AI model utilization across different providers.

items.title: Developer runs public test where 2,000 people sent 6,000+ emails trying to hack AI assistant; no secrets leaked despite sophisticated prompt injection attempts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What happened after 2k people tried to hack my AI assistant
items.summary:
A developer launched a public test inviting over 2,000 participants to send more than 6,000 emails attempting to hack an AI assistant named Fiu by extracting secret information from a protected file. Despite sophisticated prompt injection attempts, including impersonation and multilingual social engineering, the AI successfully resisted all attacks without leaking any secrets.

The experiment, conducted using the Claude Opus 4.6 model known for its resistance to prompt injection, revealed that simple but clear security instructions helped the AI maintain its defenses. The test also highlighted challenges such as high API costs, account suspensions due to unusual activity, and the impact of batch processing on the AI's suspicion levels.

The developer concluded that while prompt injection remains a security concern, powerful models with proper safeguards can effectively mitigate risks. The experiment's results have increased optimism about AI security, and future tests may explore responses to ongoing interactions and the vulnerabilities of less capable models.

The platform includes features such as no-code team sharing, auto-sync powered by git/GitHub, and built-in support for agentic search and spec-driven development. Users can install the macOS app directly or run the editor locally via Node.js on other operating systems. items.title: Unconventional AI releases Un-0, an image generator using simulated coupled oscillators achieving FID 6.74 on ImageNet 64×64 with open-source weights and code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Un-0: Generating Images with Coupled Oscillators
items.summary:
Unconventional AI has introduced Un-0, an image generator that uses a simulated system of coupled oscillators to produce images. This approach, based on physical computing principles rather than traditional deep neural networks, achieves a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score of 6.74 on the ImageNet 64×64 benchmark, comparable to early leading image generation models. The team has released the model weights, training code, and evaluation tools as open source to encourage further experimentation.

Un-0 operates by simulating thousands of oscillators whose interactions are governed by learnable coupling strengths, inspired by natural synchronization phenomena like metronomes ticking in unison. This method represents a shift toward energy-efficient AI computing by leveraging physical dynamics, aiming for significant reductions in energy consumption compared to conventional GPU-based neural networks. The project highlights the potential of physical dynamical systems as a substrate for modern AI workloads and marks a step toward more sustainable AI technologies.

A benchmark study compares the runtime performance and resource usage of four AI gateways—GoModel, LiteLLM, Portkey, and Bifrost—focusing on metrics such as request path latency, throughput, memory consumption, CPU usage, cold start time, and image size. The evaluation isolates the gateways' overhead by using a consistent mock backend and standardized testing environment to measure their efficiency on the critical request path rather than feature sets or provider coverage.

The analysis highlights that while latency differences may be minor compared to model inference times, factors like memory footprint, CPU load, cold start speed, and deployment size significantly impact operational feasibility, especially in high-volume or resource-constrained scenarios. The benchmark does not assess broader features or provider support but emphasizes the importance of runtime footprint for deploying AI gateways effectively in various environments.

items.originalTitle: AI coding agents could soon cost more than the developers using them
items.summary:
Gartner has warned that the costs of AI coding agents, driven by consumption-based pricing and limited cost control features, could surpass developer salaries by 2028. This trend is raising concerns about the financial sustainability of integrating AI tools into software development, especially as monthly bills for AI usage have escalated significantly without clear links to productivity gains.

The shift from seat-based licensing to consumption-based models has led to unpredictable and often high expenses, with some developers facing monthly charges in the thousands of dollars. Gartner highlights the lack of transparency and cost optimization tools from AI vendors, urging development teams to adopt strategies like context engineering and model routing to manage token consumption and improve output quality.

This situation is particularly impactful in regions with lower developer salaries, where AI coding costs may already match or exceed earnings. Gartner's analysis suggests that without improved cost management and vendor support, the economic balance between AI tool expenses and developer compensation could become unsustainable in the near future.

items.title: Princeton researchers develop AI system that designs radio-frequency integrated circuits, reducing design time and surpassing human performance [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Learns the "Dark Art" of RFIC Design
items.summary:
Princeton researchers have developed an artificial intelligence system that designs radio-frequency integrated circuits (RFICs), a task traditionally reliant on expert intuition and experience. This AI-driven approach uses reinforcement learning and inverse design techniques to rapidly generate RFIC layouts, achieving performance that surpasses human-designed circuits while significantly reducing design time.

The AI system overcomes the complexity of RFIC design, which involves multiple physical domains and competing optimization priorities governed by Maxwell's equations and thermodynamics. By freeing the design process from human constraints and templates, the AI produces novel circuit layouts that can accelerate advancements in wireless technologies such as 5G, autonomous vehicles, and satellite communications.

This breakthrough suggests a future where AI could become the standard for RFIC design, potentially transforming the development of wireless devices and enabling faster innovation. Continued progress will depend on creating large, shared datasets and open ecosystems to help AI systems learn universal electromagnetic and circuit behaviors.

items.summary:

The tool assesses seven key discovery layers that influence how AI systems find, understand, and recommend websites, providing a comprehensive score and actionable recommendations without requiring user registration.

The GEO checker analyzes elements including plain-text files, JSON-LD schemas, machine-readable APIs, standardized API specifications, agent-to-agent discovery files, service liveness checks, and traditional web standards. This approach helps businesses optimize their presence for generative AI search engines, a process referred to as generative engine optimization (GEO), which parallels traditional SEO but focuses on AI-driven discovery and recommendation.

Users can scan any website to receive a detailed breakdown of their GEO score with letter grades from A to F, enabling them to track improvements over time. The service is offered free indefinitely, supporting businesses in enhancing their visibility within emerging AI search platforms.

The company will initially provide access to a limited group of customers pre-approved by the US government and plans to gradually expand availability in coordination with the administration. OpenAI expressed that this government approval process is temporary and hopes to make the models widely accessible in the coming weeks.

This delay comes amid increased government scrutiny of advanced AI technologies, following an executive order aimed at addressing cybersecurity concerns related to powerful AI models. The White House's request follows similar actions taken against Anthropic, which temporarily took its most advanced AI models offline. OpenAI's GPT-5.6 models include three versions—Sol, Terra, and Luna—with enhanced capabilities and safeguards designed to prevent misuse, particularly in cybersecurity contexts.

The situation reflects growing tensions between AI innovation and regulatory oversight, as the US government seeks to balance technological advancement with national security. OpenAI's cooperation with the administration marks a cautious approach to releasing cutting-edge AI, while the broader framework for government involvement in AI model deployment remains under development.

items.originalTitle: Anthropic’s Mythos mess is only getting worse
items.summary:
Anthropic has kept its Mythos-class AI models offline for two weeks following a Trump administration export control order that barred access to these models by any foreign nationals due to security concerns. Despite sending executives to negotiate in Washington, DC, the company has not provided updates, and the talks remain unresolved, leaving the timeline for the models' return unclear. This standoff highlights challenges in applying export controls to AI technology and has significant implications for Anthropic and the broader US AI industry.

The export control order, issued on June 12th, restricts access to Mythos 5 and Fable 5 models for non-US citizens, including Anthropic employees, forcing the company to suspend the models entirely. The dispute partly stems from the lack of a clear regulatory framework for AI export controls and concerns raised after a vulnerability in Fable 5 was flagged, reportedly by Amazon CEO Andy Jassy. Security experts have argued that the identified vulnerability is overstated and represents a necessary function for AI in cybersecurity.

The ongoing impasse has affected Anthropic's financial prospects, as Mythos models were expected to drive revenue ahead of an IPO and support costly infrastructure deals. The situation also creates uncertainty in the global AI market, as the US government signals a readiness to impose similar restrictions on other AI companies, potentially reshaping industry dynamics and regulatory approaches.

items.originalTitle: An AI model programmed nonstop for 19 days on a single MirrorCode task that cost $2,600 to run
items.summary:
Epoch AI and METR have launched the MirrorCode benchmark to assess AI models' ability to recreate entire software programs without access to the original source code. Claude Opus 4.7 leads the benchmark with a 56% success rate, notably reimplementing a 16,000-line bioinformatics toolkit in 14 hours. Despite these advances, the most complex tasks remain unsolved by any model, with one AI running continuously for 19 days on a single task at a cost of $2,600.

The benchmark includes 25 programs across various domains such as Unix utilities, cryptography, and compression, requiring AI-generated solutions to match original program outputs exactly. While smaller programs are reliably handled, larger and more complex tasks still challenge current AI capabilities. The researchers note that although some models may have encountered the original code during training, memorization does not fully explain their performance. MirrorCode remains an open-source project, encouraging further development in AI-driven software reconstruction.

items.title: Analysis: Current AI boom echoes 1980s AI winter with overpromises and potential for a similar market downturn despite large-scale investments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Echoes of the AI Winter
items.summary:
The article draws parallels between the current surge in artificial intelligence, driven by large language models, and the AI boom of the 1980s that ended in the AI winter. It highlights how both periods were marked by high expectations and significant investments, followed by disillusionment when the technology failed to meet ambitious promises. Despite the impressive capabilities of today's AI systems, the article cautions that the current hype may similarly lead to a market downturn due to overpromises and oversimplifications.

The 1980s AI boom saw substantial funding for specialized hardware like Lisp machines and rule-based expert systems, which ultimately became obsolete as general-purpose microprocessors advanced rapidly. This historical context serves as a warning that the present AI enthusiasm, fueled by investments on a scale comparable to national GDPs, might not result in the transformative societal changes often predicted. The article suggests that while AI tools like large language models are valuable, the broader expectations for AI's impact should be tempered by the lessons of past technology cycles.

items.originalTitle: Notion killing Skiff-influenced email app since most users use AI agents instead
items.summary:
Notion announced it will shut down Notion Mail, its email client influenced by the Skiff acquisition, on September 22, 2026. The company cited that most users now rely on AI agents to manage their email workflows instead of opening their inboxes directly. Notion plans to focus on enhancing these AI agents to handle email management more effectively.

Notion Mail was launched in April 2025 using technology and personnel from Skiff, an encrypted email startup acquired by Notion in 2024. While Notion Mail lacked Skiff's end-to-end encryption focus, it integrated AI capabilities to personalize email handling. Users are advised to export drafts and scheduled emails before the shutdown, though most email data will remain accessible in Gmail. Organizations requiring HIPAA compliance must transition off Notion Mail by June 30, 2026.

Despite discontinuing Notion Mail, Notion may continue to leverage Skiff's technology and expertise in other productivity areas such as calendars and storage to compete with platforms like Google Workspace. The move reflects a broader shift toward AI-driven email management rather than traditional email clients.

items.summary:

These overcharges, identified through Vaudit's software that compares AI usage data with invoices, included billing for older models as if they were newer and charges for incomplete or failed AI requests. items.originalSummary:
Some customers may be paying more for Anthropic and OpenAI products than they should be due to billing inaccuracies, according to data from Vaudit, which sells an AI bill-auditing tool.

Between March and June, Vaudit audited bills sent to 60 companies totaling $34 million, mostly for usage of Anthropic’s Claude Code, and found about $1.7 million in mistaken overcharges, CEO Michael Hahn told me. Vaudit customers include Panasonic, HP, and Honda, he said.

“What we are observing is that enterprise AI billing has become increasingly opaque,” he said. 

Errant billing isn’t unique to AI, of course, and can be seen throughout enterprise software, cloud services and online advertising.

Common AI overcharges included customers using older, less expensive models but getting billed as if they were using newer, more expensive ones, Hahn said. In other cases, Hahn said customers were charged for instances when AI agents or chatbots didn’t complete requests or returned error messages. 

Other times customers didn’t realize that AI agents that had failed at a task were continuing to try to complete it, known as a retry storm, which added to the charges, Hahn said.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the company does not charge customers for incomplete requests or when they receive error messages, does not route customer requests to older models, and that overbilling doesn’t appear to be a widespread issue. An OpenAI spokesperson said it has no evidence any of those issues are happening among its customers.

Some of the customers Vaudit audited paid for access to Anthropic and OpenAI models through large cloud providers, Hahn said.

Following appeals by Vaudit and its customers, about 80% of the overcharges were credited back to customers by Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, Hahn said. The companies have been “incredibly cooperative” when these mishaps happen, he said.

AI firms have been criticized for other aspects of their billing. Last week, an Anthropic customer filed a proposed class action lawsuit against the company, alleging it misled customers about the value of its higher-priced subscription tiers. While many customers have been happy to pay up for Anthropic’s market-leading models, some are cutting costs by using cheaper or open-source models.

Vaudit, a 30-person startup founded in 2023, sells software that customers install in their AI “environment,” usually through a software developer kit, which captures raw data about customers’ AI usage to compare with invoices and billing records. 

Hahn, a former Oracle director, started Vaudit as an auditor of bills related to logistics, shipping, advertising and cloud services. It launched its AI bill auditing tool earlier this year. The startup says it charges a fee of 1% of the value of the bills it reviews and an additional 30% on refunds issued following its audits.

items.originalTitle: Citi Pitches a Cleanup for Murky SPV Market
items.summary:
Citigroup has introduced a blockchain-based service that issues tokenized depository receipts to enable clearer ownership tracking and trading of private tech company shares, initially targeting foreign investors. This initiative aims to address the complex and often unclear ownership structures arising from special purpose vehicles (SPVs) used in secondary share sales of private startups. The service requires explicit company consent and currently has one participant, Kaleido, a blockchain technology provider.

The depository receipts will carry unique serial numbers to ensure transparent ownership records on both blockchain and traditional market systems, helping companies maintain control and visibility over their shareholder base. While the service is designed to reduce risks associated with unauthorized trading and improve investor confidence, its adoption depends on private companies opting in, which may limit initial uptake. Citi plans to expand the offering to the U.S. market in the future, pending regulatory compliance and internal approvals.

items.originalSummary:
Citigroup wants to tackle the murky ownership problems that have proliferated among private tech firms as more special purpose vehicles have popped up promising to connect investors with the hottest startups. 

The bank this month said it is launching a new service that lets investors trade private company shares on a blockchain. It’s initially limited to foreign investors—it will expand to the U.S. later. And Citi needs the companies to agree. So far one firm has done so. 

That firm is Kaleido, a technology provider for enterprises to use blockchains, which has an interest in the concept. Still, if other private tech firms embrace Citi’s idea, that could expand investor access to the sector—even as it helps companies avoid the risks of unauthorized trading in their shares. 

The way the service works is that Citi will issue depository receipts—a security used for companies to access foreign investors—for private companies. It will apply a serial number for each security so ownership can be clearly tracked and transferred on both the blockchain and existing market infrastructures. 

The pitch is timely. As startups stay private longer, a cottage industry of brokers and platforms for secondary share sales has cropped up, selling interests in private companies through layers of special purpose vehicles. Some of these options have gotten so complex that it’s unclear what investors actually own. Meanwhile, many private companies ban trading in their stock without approval to avoid losing control and visibility into their ownership. 

Anthropic recently spooked some investors by warning them it won’t recognize sales of Anthropic stock its board hasn’t approved. It advised people to beware of stock scams and encouraged them to report potential frauds. 

With Citi’s private company tokens, investors “will have legal, verifiable certainty that the underlying [asset] behind those is the actual shares in the company, with the consent of the company, directly on the cap table,” said Artem Korenyuk, the bank’s global lead for digital assets enterprise alignment and services enablement. “That’s the fundamental difference that you do not get when you invest through these multilayered third-party SPVs.” 

Citi said it will get explicit permission from each company before offering its shares on the blockchain. “We don’t want to go against the company’s desires or intent,” said Korenyuk. 

That could be a big hurdle. The hottest startups may not see the need to opt into Citi’s service, and the companies that are willing to test the waters may not be the most popular names.

Some public companies have decided to tokenize their shares: but so far they have been crypto-adjacent firms like Galaxy Digital and Figure Technology. Companies whose shares are heavily sought after, such as Apple or Tesla, haven’t done so.

Still, Korenyuk believes large private companies will have incentives to opt in. Citi, acting as an agent and custodian, will show up as one line item on the company’s cap table, allowing it to clean up its cap table without losing control of and visibility into who owns its shares. Founders and shareholders can use the depository receipts as collateral to borrow money. And Citi is working to bring the service to the U.S. in the future, though it doesn’t have a timeline for that. 

“There’s internal approval that Citi has to go through,” he said. “And there are more specific implementation models that are more suitable for the U.S. market to comply with existing rules that need to be built out.”

Tech leaders from Elon Musk and Jensen Huang to a slew of startup founders and their venture-capitalist backers say robotics is headed for a “ChatGPT moment” where AI enables a wide range of physical world tasks. But the industry is increasingly split on how to get there.

At issue is which kind of AI models are most promising for powering robots. On one side are proponents of vision-language-action models, or VLAs, which are essentially derivatives of the large language models powering AI chatbots that have been trained to control robots.

On the other side are backers of world models, which are trained—often using video—to predict what will happen in a physical environment as a robot takes actions. Enthusiasm for world models has been mounting in Silicon Valley of late. This month, the AI video startup Luma launched a physical AI lab focused on world models for robotics, and the humanoid startup 1X announced its own world model lab.
